summary: Discusses the basic requirements for replicating data that is accessible through LDAPv3. It is meant as a gathering place for general replication needs so directories from different vendors can interoperate.

eli5.summary: If many copies of a phone book exist, they must stay matching. This document lists what is needed so directories from different makers can copy data to each other.

subtitle: How multiple directory servers synchronize and stay consistent with each other.

tldr.problem: LDAPv3 directory servers can be distributed across a network for reliability and performance, but when multiple servers hold copies of the same directory data, they can become inconsistent if updates happen at different times in different places.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines requirements for replication protocols that can synchronize directory data between servers, covering single-master (one server writes, others read) and multi-master (many servers can write) topologies, conflict detection, and consistency models that accept temporary mismatches as long as data eventually converges.
tldr.outcome: The document enabled vendors to implement interoperable directory replication, supporting both simple deployment patterns (single master, read-only copies) and complex ones (multiple sites updating independently), with tools to detect and repair inconsistencies when they occur.

today: RFC 3384 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definitive statement of requirements for LDAP replication interoperability. While later standards work has addressed specific replication protocols and mechanisms, the fundamental requirements in this document continue to guide LDAP directory deployments, particularly in multi-vendor enterprise environments.

sections.title: Introduction to LDAP Replication
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) is a standard way for clients to query and update directory information—employee records, organizational structure, certificates, and network configuration. Distributing directory data across multiple servers provides two key benefits: fault tolerance (if one server fails, others continue serving data) and proximity (clients can query a nearby server instead of crossing the network).

While RFC 2251 (LDAPv3 core) defines how clients talk to servers and mentions shadow servers (read-only copies), it does not specify a replication mechanism. Different vendors implemented different approaches, breaking interoperability. This document sets out the requirements for a standard LDAP replication protocol so that servers from different makers can synchronize directory data reliably.
sections.eli5: Directory servers are like librarians keeping lists of information. Sometimes you need more than one librarian so they can help more people at once, but they all need to have the same books. This part explains why standardized copying is necessary.

sections.title: Data Consistency Models
sections.content:
The RFC considers five theoretical consistency models. Model 1 (Transactional Consistency with ACID guarantees) would require expensive distributed two-phase commit and is deferred for future work. Model 4 (Loosest Consistency—a cache until stale) and Model 5 (Ad hoc—no follow-up checks) do not use prearranged agreements and violate directory security policies.

Instead, requirements focus on Models 2 and 3. Model 2 (Eventual Consistency) assumes all servers know the replication topology in advance via replication agreements. Every update eventually propagates to every replica it can reach. Model 3 (Limited Effort Eventual Consistency) is similar but allows updates to be purged if they exceed an age boundary, leaving some changes replicated to only some servers. Both models accept temporary mismatches: immediately after an update at one server, a different server might have the old value, but they converge over time.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to keep copies in sync. Some methods guarantee perfect agreement every second (but are expensive). Others accept that copies might differ temporarily but promise they will eventually match. This document focuses on the practical ones.

sections.title: Single-Master and Multi-Master Replication
sections.content:
In single-master replication (also called master-slave), one server is the authoritative source for write operations. All updates go to the master; other servers are read-only replicas. When the master changes data, those changes flow to the slaves. This model is simpler because there is no conflict to resolve: if two updates arrive at the slaves at different times, it does not matter because the master's order is the canonical one.

In multi-master replication, multiple servers can accept write operations independently. This offers better availability—if the master goes down, clients can still update data on another master—but creates challenges. If two servers apply different updates to the same data before replicating, they have a conflict. The protocol must detect conflicts, resolve them deterministically (e.g., timestamp-based or unique-identifier-based), and ensure that all servers eventually agree on a result without losing information.
sections.eli5: Imagine a phone book. One approach: one person updates the master copy, and others send copies of it to all offices. Another approach: any office can update its copy, and they all send changes to each other. The second is more flexible but much trickier to manage.

sections.title: Partial Replication and Schema Flexibility
sections.content:
Fractional replication allows a server to replicate only a subset of attributes from an entry (e.g., employee name and phone number but not salary). Sparse replication replicates only a subset of entries from an area of replication. These partial approaches are useful when different sites need different data or when bandwidth is limited.

Directory schemas vary between vendors. When replicating between servers with different schemas, the protocol must handle mismatches: raising an error, converting data to the target schema, or skipping unknown attributes. The requirements support all approaches and recommend that vendors provide tools to detect schema compatibility before replication is set up. The replication protocol itself must be able to handle unexpected mismatches discovered during synchronization.
sections.eli5: Not every office needs every piece of information. One office might only need phone numbers, another only email addresses. Also, different software makers use slightly different formats. The protocol must handle both situations.

sections.title: Replication Operations and Management
sections.content:
Replication can be initiated on a schedule (specific times, periodic intervals, or when a threshold of changes accumulates), on-demand (manual request), or automatically (when a critical attribute like a password is changed). A replica cycle is the exchange of updates between two servers in a replica-group (the set of servers holding the same data). Both supplier (sending updates) and consumer (receiving updates) roles must be supported, and in multi-master systems, the two servers can switch roles during a single sync cycle.

Full replication (complete resync) and incremental replication (only changes) are both required. Full replication should use a standard format like LDIF (LDAP Data Interchange Format) so new servers can be initialized from a standard backup. Each replication agreement (configuration describing which servers replicate with which) must be accessible via LDAP, and servers must be able to audit which other servers they have exchanged data with, helping administrators detect and repair inconsistencies.
sections.eli5: Servers need to know when to synchronize (on a schedule or on demand), what to send (all data or just changes), and how to handle errors if one server is unreachable. All of this setup and record-keeping must be manageable through standard LDAP queries.

sections.title: Security and Authentication
sections.content:
Directories often hold sensitive information: passwords, certificates, employee records, and business policy. Replication traffic must be protected against eavesdropping and tampering. The protocol must support mutual authentication (each server verifies the other), mutual authorization (each verifies the other is allowed to replicate), and optional encryption.

In some cases (e.g., between corporate partners in an extranet), anonymous replication (endpoints identified but not authenticated) may be acceptable. The protocol must support this and also allow authenticated sources and replicas to agree to disable confidentiality for a specific session (e.g., if both are on a private network). There must be at least one mandatory-to-implement confidentiality mechanism and one for integrity, so different vendors' implementations can always communicate securely.
sections.eli5: Copying directory data across the network is risky. Eavesdroppers might capture passwords, and attackers might try to inject fake updates. The protocol must verify that both servers are trusted, keep the data secret, and prevent tampering. But it also needs to let different vendors use their preferred encryption method.
